title: RL-Trader: Generalization and Evaluation Rigor in Deep Reinforcement Learning
description:
Deep reinforcement learning is unusually easy to fool yourself with: agents memorize their training trajectory, and a single lucky random seed can masquerade as a real result. This work studies both failure modes from scratch — a PyTorch implementation of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), two custom Gymnasium environments, and a full evaluation suite — using financial markets as a deliberately hard testbed: non-stationary, partially observable, with a noisy reward and near–random-walk signal.

The headline result is negative, and that is the point: on real markets the agent has no seed-robust edge over buy-and-hold, and the project's own significance tooling catches a single-seed “+275%” run as a false positive. The work introduces a surrogate-data falsification test that separates “the agent is weak” from “there is no signal to find,” validated with a positive control on synthetic data with known structure.

In doing so it reproduces, in a new domain, the central methodological finding of Henderson et al. (2018) — that single-run RL evaluation is unreliable — and then applies that finding to its own ablation, which is run on simulated market paths and reports both arms as distributions over ten seeds where all four confidence intervals exclude zero.

The study was then audited against current deep-RL evaluation practice in pre-registered experiments. The audit found two real flaws: the from-scratch PPO trailed Stable-Baselines3 on two of four standard benchmarks, and the crypto train/test split leaked across coins in calendar time. Both are fixed, and neither changes the conclusion: no implementation, algorithm (PPO, SAC), training budget up to 1M steps, or hindsight-free stock universe beats buy-and-hold. A second pre-registered study ran 30 seeds and retrained the whole basket across four periods of history. On stocks the agent trails buy-and-hold in all 300 runs and in every period. On crypto it trails on five of six coins (not significant with six coins, p = 0.19) and in three of four periods, the exception being a crash it lost less in. Its long-or-short calls match the next day's move 50.0% of the time, and the trading costs of reversing them daily are about the size of its negative alpha.

Part 2 turns the same PPO to a problem reinforcement learning is suited to: hedging a short option when every trade costs money. Theory gives two answers to check against (the Black-Scholes delta with free trading, a widening no-trade band with costs). The agent, trained only on simulated paths, tracks delta within about 0.04 shares without observing it (scoring slightly below it), learns to trade less as costs rise, and on 237 real one-month SPY episodes (2007–2026) it never trained on, ties a tuned no-trade-band hedge at low costs and beats it at 0.2% and 1% costs (9/10 and 10/10 seeds).
notes: Version 2.3.0. Pre-registered audit (docs/preregistration/2026-11-13-rigor.md, RESULTS.md section 10): the PPO repaired to match Stable-Baselines3 on 3 of 4 benchmarks (now the default; RL_TRADER_PUBLISHED=1 restores 2.2.1), a leak-free calendar split for crypto, headline results regenerated, and checks across implementations, SAC, budgets to 1M steps and a hindsight-free Dow 2016 universe, with Holm-adjusted p-values. Added later: a hardware replication and risk-adjusted results (Sharpe, alpha, beta; RESULTS.md 5d-5e), and a second pre-registered study (docs/preregistration/2026-11-14-depth.md, RESULTS.md 10h): 30 seeds, walk-forward over the whole basket in four periods, the hyper-parameter sweep at 10 seeds and the full budget (0 of 18 configurations beat buy-and-hold), and position diagnostics. Five of its six predictions held; one failed (crypto in the 2025-26 crash). Also: the ablation is labelled as run on simulated paths, a weekly job tests the hedging agent on real option quotes, and a one-page plain-English summary. Version 2.2.1. Adds Part 2, an option-hedging study (rl_trader/hedging, RESULTS.md section 9, paper RQ5): the same PPO trained on simulated paths, checked against the Black-Scholes delta and a no-trade band, and tested on 237 real one-month SPY episodes against a band tuned per cost. Also corrects the prose around the generated tables (RESULTS.md, the paper, the README and the site), which still described the 5-seed ablation after it moved to 10 seeds, and still called the domain-randomized arm unseeded after it was seeded in 2.1. Those passages now match the tables, the paper's Table 2 caption says 10 seeds, the multi-fold walk-forward is reported rather than listed as future work, and a test fails if the prose quotes a stale seed count again. Every number in Part 1 is unchanged. Version 2.2.0. The domain-randomization arm of the ablation now draws its training paths from a stream fixed by the training seed (rl_trader.data.seeded_path_factory); before, it drew from OS entropy, so no single domain-randomized run could be reproduced. The ablation was re-run with the fix and extended from 5 to 10 seeds: held-out return for the domain arm is +31% [+21, +44] on stocks (was +47% [+31, +64]) and +187% [+147, +229] on crypto (was +129% [+82, +185]); single-path is -25% [-33, -15] and -44% [-59, -21]. All four confidence intervals still exclude zero, so the paper's conclusion is unchanged. From 2.0.0: Every published figure was regenerated against a pinned data snapshot (data/SNAPSHOT.json, window ending 2026-08-28) rather than a rolling window, which is what makes the numbers reproducible. Rebuilding the identical recipe on the later window changed the headline single-seed crypto result from +275% to +38.7%, so v1's figures are superseded rather than corrected; v1 remains available at commit d4c0ef9. Result tables in the README, RESULTS.md and the paper are generated from the committed artifacts by tools/sync_docs.py and checked by the test suite, so the documents cannot drift from the experiments. Source, figures and the full evaluation suite are in the linked repository.
